title: Trade and honesty
hookLine: the honest merchant is with the prophets (Tirmidhi)

lines: A HEAP OF GRAIN IN MEDINA.
cards: A market in Medina. Grain is heaped up for sale, dry and golden on top. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is walking past, and he pushes his hand down into the pile.
His fingers come out wet. The seller says the rain got to it. Then why not put the wet part on top, the Prophet asks, so people can see it?
And he says: whoever cheats is not of me. Today: trade, and the one thing a market can't run without.

teach.h: THE MARKET IS NOT A DIRTY PLACE.
teach.b: In these texts the market isn't a dirty place. Tradition says the Prophet himself worked in trade before his mission, and the Qur'an mentions the caravans of winter and summer without embarrassment.
What it watches is the scale.
Surah eighty-three opens, in Pickthall's words, "Woe unto the defrauders," people who demand full measure when they buy and give short measure when they sell. Then the reward.

teach.h: WITH THE PROPHETS AND THE MARTYRS.
teach.b: In a report in Tirmidhi, the Prophet says the truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs.
Someone who sells phone cases, or tomatoes, or used cars, in that company, for telling the truth about the goods. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari makes it practical.
Buyer and seller keep the right to back out until they part.

teach.h: SPEAK TRULY, AND MAKE IT CLEAR.
teach.b: If both speak truly and make things clear, their sale is blessed; if they hide things and lie, its blessing is wiped out. Two verbs: speak truly, and make clear. Not lying is half.
The other half is the grain story: showing the flaw before the buyer finds it. That's why the fiqh books give buyers a right to return goods with a hidden defect the seller didn't mention.
Honesty isn't left to the seller's mood; the law builds it into the contract. The honest merchant isn't a saint who wandered into a market. It's someone who puts the wet grain on top.

how: Muslim merchants are taught to disclose defects, give full measure and avoid false oaths in selling, and Islamic law gives buyers a right to return goods with a hidden defect.

o: fixing a fair price so that no seller makes too much profit
letting the buyer beware, since a sale is final once agreed
honest dealing: speaking truly and showing a flaw before it's found

games.q: trade and honesty — tap the pairs.
p: full measure in, short measure out
with the prophets and the martyrs
gives the buyer a right to return

s: Islam treats trade as a lower, worldly business
the honest merchant is promised the company of the prophets.
the Prophet said a sale is blessed when both sides speak truly and make things clear
the report in Bukhari says lying and hiding wipe the blessing out.
not lying is enough to count as an honest seller
the report pairs speaking truly with making things clear: showing the flaw too.

games.q: you're selling grain in Medina. the rain soaked part of it. the Prophet pushes his hand in and finds it wet. what does he say you should have done?
o: sold it at a lower price without saying why.
put the wet part on top where people could see it.
games.why: he asks why the wet part wasn't on top so people could see it, and says whoever cheats is not of him.

practice: Replay the last thing you sold, traded or recommended: a couch online, an old phone, a pitch at work, a review you left. Was what you said true, and did the flaw get shown before anyone had to find it?
No grading, just looking; if you pray, you can ask for honesty in the next one.

wordCard.voice: Trade and honesty. In Islam, trade is honorable, and a sale is blessed when both sides speak truly and make the flaws clear. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: truthfulness; the quality of the truthful merchant.

carryVoice: Your line: the honest merchant. Speak truly, and make it clear. Same time tomorrow.
